cells.tense: Right now you're holding the weight and the care at the same time, and the pen is still in your hand.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending, say out loud how long it needs, and hold only that.
cells.core:
You're carrying something heavy and staying in touch with what's alive in it. That's harder than either part alone, and it's working — the bearing has softened instead of hardened, and the care hasn't drained you dry. You're not squeezing anything to grow faster than it will, and you're not letting go to prove you don't need it. Both of those would be easier. You're doing neither.

What that buys you is room to be pulled forward by something instead of spending your days bracing. A thing worth releasing is already reaching its finish, and the release you have in you now is a fullness, not a defeat. Let one small thing complete this week — a project, a plan, a bottle of whatever is sitting half-finished — and say out loud, in your own words, what it was for. That's the kind of release that makes space rather than takes it.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the weight and stay soft inside it, and you choose both.
cells.verb: tending what's growing — giving it conditions, not commands
cells.place: the long middle of a hard thing, where you hold and keep holding

cells.tense: You're braced for a future that hasn't arrived yet, and most of your holding is aimed past the present.
cells.ask: Choose one thing you've been gripping and put it down for a day; write down what actually happens.
cells.core:
You're caring for what's growing by reaching ahead of it — arranging, deciding, keeping the next room ready. That's love with the gloves on, and it works right up until the thing that's growing feels the grip and stiffens. The weight you're carrying has stopped being only what's here and started including what might be. No amount of arranging writes anyone's future in for them.

The self-check question is whether you can sit down with a thing that's mid-flight and not touch it. Pick one thing you've decided you know how it should go, and let it run a day the way it runs when you're not there — no calls, no fixing, no reading the room. Then write one page about what happened without you. You may find that the shape it takes on its own is one you could actually enjoy, not merely supervise. The next step is often enough; the whole road isn't.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding what hasn't happened yet, and it's costing you what's here.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you, holding a load you stopped handing to anyone.
cells.ask: Tend one thing of your own for twenty minutes today — and tell one person it's yours.
cells.core:
You can carry what needs carrying, and you've carried a lot — but that work has gone quiet, and it stopped reaching anyone, including yourself. That's not independence. It's a lamp that stopped being lit and got renamed as not needing one. What's growing near you still gets what it needs to survive. Nothing gets what it needs to open.

You don't fix this by feeling more, or by pushing care into a part of you that's run down — that's how it goes stale. You fix it by starting one small thing that's nobody's but yours, and letting the point of it be the point of it. Twenty minutes, a stretch of soil, a draft, a corner, and one sentence to someone: 'this one's mine.' What you get out of it isn't the whole road lit; it's enough light to take the next step.
cells.sheetLine: You can carry it, and you've stopped tending anything of your own.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you're already writing in — people are being held, fed, kept, and you've stopped counting it as yours.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're carrying for someone, say aloud whose decision it was to take it on, and hand one back.
cells.core:
You're carrying a lot for other people, and you weren't the one who signed up for all of it. From the outside that reads as care. From the inside it's depletion — you're in the caretaker seat and nobody, including you, said you picked it. The work is real. What's gone missing is the plain fact of who decided it.

What's harder than saying yes is noticing which yeses you didn't say. Pick one thing you're currently carrying and find the moment it became yours — if you can't, that's your answer. Say out loud who decided it, including the ones where the honest answer is no one. Then let one thing finish and come off your hands, as a completion, not a failure. What you put down stops being weight and starts being room.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying what you didn't agree to carry, and it's time to say so.

cells.place: the long middle of a hard thing, where you hold and keep holding
